scope: Five recurring historical written forms without recognized current-engine analysis; cited lexical reference leads, not Gold or Silver, no change to the published translator.
source_policy: Historical source references and their printed locations/secondary edition named; source gloss leads are not automatic per-stanza semantic translations.

recorded.source_locator: James Lockhart, Nahuatl as Written (2001), p. 242; ODN yehuantin records yehuan short-form variant
recorded.lead: short emphatic 3rd-person plural pronoun; contextual address/referent is unresolved
recorded.contextual_caveat: In Brinton expressions such as yehuan Dios the pronoun scope and archaic poetic syntax cannot be solved by inserting 'they' mechanically; separate printed occurrences need source-sensitive grammar review.

recorded.source_locator: Alonso de Molina, Vocabulario (1571), Nahuatl-to-Spanish part II f.103r col.1; Lockhart discussion via ODN tepiltzin
recorded.lead: children, offspring; in certain social contexts, noble or chiefly offspring/young people
recorded.contextual_caveat: The source supports a form and multiple possible social senses; the broader poetic audience cannot automatically be translated as literal children.

recorded.source_family: Lockhart / Molina via Online Nahuatl Dictionary
recorded.source_locator: Lockhart, Nahuatl as Written (2001) p.242, possessed -yollo; Molina (1571) II f.40v for yollotl
recorded.lead: my heart, spirit, state of mind (possessed heart-expression)
recorded.contextual_caveat: A lexical/possessive source gloss is not proof of whether a given poetic phrase means heart, mind, intention or soul.

recorded.source_locator: Wimmer (2004) entry ipalnemohua, divine title/verbal expression; UNAM indexed context Sahagun Book 6
recorded.lead: he by whom one lives; divine epithet, sometimes idiomatically Giver of Life
recorded.contextual_caveat: Do not treat the form as an arbitrary inflection of a known verb or equate it with all related divine names without source analysis.

recorded.source_locator: ODN huiya entry, inflected form from yauh 'go'; compare Brinton 1890 song stanzas xiii.9, xv.2, xv.13 and xvii.15
recorded.lead: historical dictionary records verbal went; repeated song-position uses may instead be sung interjection and must be individually differentiated
recorded.contextual_caveat: A dictionary form alone must not override poetic placement, and a refrain-like position does not prove the form is never a finite verb; leave unresolved.
